title: Consistency models in practice: quorums (N, R, W), staleness and PACELC
description: Measure every (R, W) setting of a 3-replica store on a seeded simulated network - latency, stale reads, read-your-writes, new-then-old inversions, availability with a region down - and choose one per use case; R + W > N turns out not to be linearizable until you add read write-back.
outcome: You can place linearizable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency on a map, measure what each quorum setting costs (PACELC), decide per use case from evidence, and make a quorum register linearizable with read write-back.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional: Maelstrom 0.2.4 (JDK 11+) for the lin-kv exercise (manual).
overview: Consistency is a menu with prices: measure staleness, anomalies, latency and availability per setting, then choose per use case and record why.
prerequisites: Lesson 9 (consistent hashing: N replicas per key)

designBrief.context: One replicated key-value store (N = 3: zones A and B in one region, zone C in another) serves a cart badge, feature flags and a lock-owner/config key. A single writer updates each key; readers sit in all three zones; 5% of messages hit a 20-80 ms slow tail.
constraints: Cart badge: <= 20% stale reads, read p99 <= 70 ms, write p99 <= 40 ms, >= 99% answered with region C down
Feature flags: <= 1% stale reads, 0 read-your-writes violations, read p99 <= 80 ms, write p99 <= 100 ms, >= 99% answered with region C down
Lock owner / config: linearizable (0 stale, 0 inversions), read p99 <= 150 ms, write p99 <= 100 ms, >= 99% answered with region C down
designBrief.question: Which N, R, W (and read write-back or not) does each use case get?

options.name: R=1 W=1 (eventual)
options.description: Fastest single replica answers reads and acknowledges writes.
options.evidence: read p99 60.5 ms, write p99 34.0 ms, 16.74% stale (max age 86.9 ms), 15 read-your-writes violations, 902 inversions, 100% answered with region C down
options.verdict: Chosen for the cart badge only.

options.name: R=2 W=2 (R + W > N)
options.description: Overlapping quorums, newest of two replies.
options.evidence: read p99 65.9 ms, write p99 68.3 ms, 0% stale, 0 read-your-writes violations, 2 inversions (not linearizable), 100% answered with region C down
options.verdict: Chosen for feature flags; not enough for config.

options.name: R=2 W=2 + read write-back (ABD)
options.description: A read writes the newest value back to W replicas before returning, when replicas disagree.
options.evidence: read p50 12.7 ms, read p99 124.5 ms, write p99 67.5 ms, 0 stale, 0 inversions (linearizable), 100% answered with region C down; R=3 W=1 is also linearizable but answers 0% with C down

fitnessFunction.what: The config setting (N=3 R=2 W=2 + read write-back) stays linearizable, fast enough and available when a region is lost.
fitnessFunction.threshold: 0 stale reads and 0 inversions on seeds 11-20; read p99 <= 150 ms; >= 99% of reads and writes answered with region C down

scalingLimits: Larger N or replicas further away: R and W wait for the slowest member of the quorum, so p99 rises with every cross-region replica (signal: read/write p99 tracks the far replica's RTT).

Many writers per key: the single-writer version numbers no longer order writes; you need (counter, writer id) versions or a consensus log (signal: concurrent writes with equal versions, lost updates).
Sloppy quorums / hinted handoff during failures break R + W > N overlap (signal: stale reads appear only during node failures).

glossary.meaning: Every operation appears to take effect at one instant between its start and end; once any read sees a value, every later read sees it or newer.
One total order consistent with each client's order (not real time) / effects never seen before their causes; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders.
N replicas; a write waits for W acknowledgements, a read for R replies; R + W > N makes every read quorum overlap every write quorum.
If Partition: Availability vs Consistency; Else: Latency vs Consistency (Abadi 2012).
Second phase of a quorum read (Attiya, Bar-Noy, Dolev): store the newest value on W replicas before returning it.

concepts: R + W > N prevents stale reads of finished writes, not new-then-old between concurrent reads.
The latency/consistency trade-off is paid on every request, the availability trade-off only during partitions.
Choose per use case, from measured numbers, and keep the choice true with a test.

codeWalkthrough.title: Write path
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Cluster.write` fans out to all N replicas; each applies `max(version)` and acks; the write succeeds at the W-th ack (Dynamo: latency = W-th fastest replica) or fails at the 300 ms timeout.

codeWalkthrough.title: Read path
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Cluster.read` asks all N and uses the first R replies; `finish_read` returns the newest of them. The lesson ignores `write_back`, so nothing guarantees later reads see that value.

codeWalkthrough.title: Workload
codeWalkthrough.detail: `run` drives a closed-loop writer (write v+1, then read it back) and six readers in zones A, B, C on a seeded simulated network; ops started after `run_ms` are not started, in-flight ones drain.

codeWalkthrough.title: History checks
codeWalkthrough.detail: `helpers.anomalies` sweeps the history once: stale (older than a write finished before the read began), inversion (older than an already finished read), read-your-writes. For a single-writer register, no stale and no inversion means linearizable - cross-checked against the L300 #13 exhaustive checker.

codeWalkthrough.title: PACELC column
codeWalkthrough.detail: `measure` re-runs the workload with replica c down and reports the worse of read and write availability.

codeWalkthrough.title: Decision as code
codeWalkthrough.detail: `USE_CASES` holds each brief's numbers; `decide` returns the fastest setting that meets them, or None - the evidence and the choice live in one place.

checkYourself.q: N=3, R=2, W=2. A write has reached replica a only; reader 1 gets a and b, reader 2 (starting after reader 1 ends) gets b and c. What do they return, and which model is violated?
checkYourself.a: Reader 1 returns the new value, reader 2 the old one: new-then-old, so not linearizable (it can still be sequentially consistent).

checkYourself.q: Why does write-back barely change p50 but double p99?
checkYourself.a: It only runs when the R replies disagree, which happens mostly while a write is in flight or delayed - the tail.

checkYourself.q: Which half of PACELC did tryIt 2 show?
checkYourself.a: The partition half: R=1 W=1 stays available (PA), R=2 W=2 refuses (PC).

title: CRDTs for local-first collaboration: counters, OR-Set, LWW-Register and property tests
description: Implement G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set and LWW-Register, test their merge laws and convergence with a seeded property-based tester that shrinks failures, and find the LWW tie that makes two replicas diverge forever.
outcome: You can choose a CRDT per field from the wanted concurrent semantics, prove merge laws with random histories, read a shrunk counterexample, and estimate metadata cost.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional: Node 24 + npm for the Automerge 3.3.2 equivalent (CI only).
overview: Local-first apps write locally and merge later; a merge that is commutative, associative and idempotent makes every replica converge no matter how the sync behaved.

designBrief.context: A shopping-list app runs on a phone and a laptop, offline for hours, syncing over an unreliable channel that loses, reorders and duplicates messages (20% of syncs are delivered twice in the lab). No server decides conflicts.
constraints: Every replica converges after anti-entropy: 500/500 seeded histories per type
Concurrent increments are never lost (a like-counter must equal the true sum)
A concurrent add and remove of the same item keeps the item (add wins)
A busy cart session ships <= 4,096 bytes per sync

scalingLimits: Tombstones are never collected: one item re-added and removed 1,000 times costs 31,813 bytes (signal: sync size grows while the visible list does not).
Counter vectors keep one slot per replica that ever wrote: many short-lived devices grow every counter (signal: state bytes per counter grow with device churn).
Global invariants (stock >= 0, unique usernames) cannot be enforced by merging local states (signal: oversold items after a merge) - they need reservations or coordination.

glossary.meaning: A replicated type whose merge is a least upper bound: commutative, associative, idempotent; replicas that saw the same updates are equal.
Observed-remove set: each add has a unique tag; a remove tombstones only the tags it saw, so a concurrent add wins.
Last-writer-wins register ordered by a timestamp; ties need a deterministic rule (replica id).
Check a law on many random inputs; on failure, remove steps while it still fails to get a minimal counterexample.

concepts: Choose the type by what should happen on concurrent updates.
Merge laws are testable properties; duplicates in the history are part of the test.
Metadata is the price: tags, tombstones, per-replica slots.

codeWalkthrough.title: G-Counter
codeWalkthrough.detail: One slot per replica; `inc` touches only its own slot; `merge` takes the per-slot max - a join on vectors, so duplicated syncs change nothing.

codeWalkthrough.title: PN-Counter
codeWalkthrough.detail: Two G-Counters (increments, decrements); value = P - N. Decrements stay monotone in N, so the join still works.

codeWalkthrough.title: OR-Set
codeWalkthrough.detail: `add` stores a unique tag; `remove` copies only the tags this replica has seen into the tombstones; value = elements with a live tag. A concurrent add has a tag the remover never saw, so it survives.

codeWalkthrough.title: LWW-Register (the bug)
codeWalkthrough.detail: `merge` keeps `other` only if `other.ts > self.ts`; on a tie each side keeps its own value, so merge(x, y) != merge(y, x).

codeWalkthrough.title: Property tester
codeWalkthrough.detail: `helpers.gen_history` mixes local updates with random, 20%-duplicated syncs; `law_failures` checks the three laws on the resulting states; `diverged` checks convergence (and the true sum for counters) after random anti-entropy.

codeWalkthrough.title: Shrinking
codeWalkthrough.detail: `helpers.shrink` removes one step at a time while the property still fails, turning a 12-step history into the 2-step tie.

codeWalkthrough.title: Options as code
codeWalkthrough.detail: `like_counter` runs the same 300 seeded updates through a last-writer-wins number and a PN-Counter and reports values and sync bytes.

code:
"""L400 lesson 19 (python multiregion.py): multi-region design under a latency budget, measured in a simulation.
Three regions (us, eu, ap; latencies in helpers.py), 100 writes/s for 20 s, seeded. Designs: single leader with
async or majority-sync replication, multi-leader, leaderless W=2. For each we measure write p99 per user region,
follower lag, write conflicts, and what a region failure at t=10 s costs: RPO (acknowledged writes lost) and RTO
(time until writes succeed again). The deployed design is checked against the constraints in the design brief."""
from helpers import REGIONS, TRAFFIC, Net, conflicts, pct, write_stream

T_FAIL, ELECTION_MS = 10000.0, (1000.0, 2000.0)  # failure time; election timeout range (WAN heartbeats)
DESIGN = {"replication": "async", "leader": "ap"}  # as deployed: the first region the team launched in
CONSTRAINTS = {"write_p99_ms": {"us": 350.0, "eu": 350.0}, "rpo_writes": 0, "rto_ms": 5000.0, "conflicts": 0}


def leader_write(net, mode, leader, followers, t, origin):
    """Single leader: one round trip to the leader; majority-sync also waits for the FIRST follower ack."""
    t_arr = net.send(origin, leader, t)
    arrive = {leader: t_arr, **{f: net.send(leader, f, t_arr, fifo=True) for f in followers}}  # the log stream
    commit = t_arr if mode == "async" else min(net.send(f, leader, arrive[f]) for f in followers)
    return t_arr, commit, net.send(leader, origin, commit), arrive


def simulate(design, seed=19, fail=False):
    net, mode, leader = Net(seed), design["replication"], design.get("leader")
    down = (leader or "us") if fail else None  # leader designs lose the leader's region; others the busiest one
    writes, rejected, log, new_leader, t_elect = [], 0, [], None, None
    for seq, (t, origin, key) in enumerate(write_stream(seed)):
        after = fail and t >= T_FAIL
        if after and origin == down:
            continue  # those users are down with their region
        w = {"t": t, "origin": origin, "key": key, "seq": seq}
        if mode in ("async", "sync-majority"):
            if after and new_leader is None:  # failover: promote the most up-to-date survivor (Raft 5.4.1)
                survivors = [r for r in REGIONS if r != down]
                has = {r: sum(x["arrive"][r] < T_FAIL for x in log) for r in survivors}  # FIFO -> log prefix
                new_leader = max(survivors, key=lambda r: has[r])
                t_elect = T_FAIL + net.rng.uniform(*ELECTION_MS) + 2 * max(net.d(*survivors), 1.0)
                lost = [x for x in log if x["commit"] < T_FAIL and x["arrive"][new_leader] >= T_FAIL]
            lead = new_leader if after else leader
            followers = [r for r in REGIONS if r != lead and not (after and r == down)]
            t_arr, w["commit"], w["ack"], w["arrive"] = leader_write(net, mode, lead, followers, t, origin)
            if (after and t_arr < t_elect) or (fail and not after and t_arr >= T_FAIL):
                rejected += 1  # no leader yet (or the request died with the old one): the write fails
                continue
            w["accepted"] = t_arr
            log.append(w)
        elif mode == "multi-leader":  # every region accepts locally, replicates asynchronously
            w["accepted"] = w["commit"] = net.send(origin, origin, t)
            w["ack"] = net.send(origin, origin, w["commit"])
            w["arrive"] = {r: w["commit"] if r == origin else net.send(origin, r, w["commit"], fifo=True) for r in REGIONS}
        else:  # leaderless: the client's region coordinates, W=2 of the 3 regions must ack
            live = [r for r in REGIONS if not (after and r == down)]
            w["arrive"] = {r: net.send(origin, r, t) for r in live}
            backs = sorted(net.send(r, origin, w["arrive"][r]) for r in live)
            w["accepted"], w["commit"] = t, backs[1]
            w["ack"] = backs[1]
            w["arrive"].update({r: float("inf") for r in REGIONS if r not in live})
        writes.append(w)
    if mode not in ("async", "sync-majority"):  # no failover needed; data only on the dead region is gone
        lost = [w for w in writes if fail and w["commit"] < T_FAIL and all(
            w["arrive"][r] >= T_FAIL for r in REGIONS if r != down)]
    before = [w for w in writes if w["t"] < T_FAIL or not fail]
    lag = [w["arrive"][r] - w["commit"] for w in before for r in REGIONS if w["arrive"][r] != float("inf")]
    first_ok = min((w["t"] for w in writes if fail and w["t"] >= T_FAIL), default=T_FAIL)  # first write that works
    return {"p99": {o: pct([w["ack"] - w["t"] for w in before if w["origin"] == o], 99) for o in REGIONS},
            "lag_p99": pct(lag, 99), "lag_p99_at": {r: pct([w["arrive"][r] - w["commit"] for w in before
                                                          if w["arrive"][r] != float("inf")], 99) for r in REGIONS},
            "conflicts": conflicts(before) if mode in ("multi-leader", "leaderless") else 0,
            "rpo_writes": len(lost) if fail else 0, "rto_ms": round(first_ok - T_FAIL) if fail else 0,
            "rejected": rejected}


def evaluate(design, seed=19):
    calm, failed = simulate(design, seed), simulate(design, seed, fail=True)
    return {**calm, "rpo_writes": failed["rpo_writes"], "rto_ms": failed["rto_ms"], "rejected": failed["rejected"]}


def violations(m):
    c = CONSTRAINTS
    out = [f"{o} write p99 {m['p99'][o]} > {lim} ms" for o, lim in c["write_p99_ms"].items() if m["p99"][o] > lim]
    out += [f"RPO: {m['rpo_writes']} acknowledged writes lost"] if m["rpo_writes"] > c["rpo_writes"] else []
    out += [f"RTO {m['rto_ms']} ms > {c['rto_ms']:.0f} ms"] if m["rto_ms"] > c["rto_ms"] else []
    return out + ([f"{m['conflicts']} write conflicts"] if m["conflicts"] > c["conflicts"] else [])


def place_leader(replication, seed=19):
    """Build task: choose the leader region by measurement (traffic-weighted write p99), not by history."""
    return DESIGN["leader"]


OPTIONS = [("async", "ap"), ("async", "us"), ("sync-majority", "us"), ("sync-majority", "eu"),
           ("sync-majority", "ap"), ("multi-leader", None), ("leaderless", None)]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("design               write p99 us / eu / ap ms   lag p99  conflicts  RPO lost  RTO ms  rejected")
    for mode, leader in OPTIONS:
        m = evaluate({"replication": mode, "leader": leader})
        print(f"{mode + ('@' + leader if leader else ''):20} {m['p99']['us']:>8} / {m['p99']['eu']:>6} / {m['p99']['ap']:>6}"
              f" {m['lag_p99']:>9} {m['conflicts']:>10} {m['rpo_writes']:>9} {m['rto_ms']:>7} {m['rejected']:>9}")
    print(f"deployed {DESIGN}: violations {violations(evaluate(DESIGN)) or 'none'}")
    print(f"place_leader('sync-majority') -> {place_leader('sync-majority')}")

codeWalkthrough.title: One write, as legs
codeWalkthrough.detail: `leader_write`: client -> leader (`t_arr`), leader -> each follower on a FIFO replication stream; async commits at `t_arr`, majority-sync at the first follower ack; the client hears back one leg later.

codeWalkthrough.title: Failover
codeWalkthrough.detail: At the first write after `T_FAIL`, the most up-to-date survivor (the longest log prefix received before the failure) becomes leader after its election timeout plus a vote round trip (`t_elect`); writes arriving earlier are rejected.

codeWalkthrough.title: RPO, measured
codeWalkthrough.detail: `lost` = writes committed before the failure that had not reached the new leader. Majority-sync makes this empty by construction - which is exactly the property to prove.

codeWalkthrough.title: Multi-leader and leaderless
codeWalkthrough.detail: Multi-leader commits locally and replicates; leaderless waits for the 2nd of 3 replies from the client's region. Neither needs failover; `helpers.conflicts` counts concurrent writes to one key from different regions.

codeWalkthrough.title: RTO, measured
codeWalkthrough.detail: `first_ok` = issue time of the first write after the failure that succeeds; RTO = first_ok - T_FAIL.

codeWalkthrough.title: Brief as code
codeWalkthrough.detail: `CONSTRAINTS` + `violations()` turn the design brief into checks; `place_leader()` is the build task: choose by traffic-weighted p99, not by history.

overview: A chaos experiment is a hypothesis test about steady state under a real-world fault - and it must be bounded, because a refuted hypothesis means someone was harmed.

designBrief.context: Lessons 12 and 14 produced a hardened Raft log and a hardened order saga. The team wants continuous evidence that they survive courier outages, orchestrator crashes, node crashes and rolling restarts - in CI, with production-like traffic later.

An experiment that refutes its hypothesis may hurt at most 1 customer (abort rule)
Order-level faults touch at most 10% of orders; the rest is a control group
Raft faults touch one node at a time (a minority)

codeWalkthrough.title: State as immutable tuples
codeWalkthrough.detail: `init()` returns (per-node (term, votedFor, role, votes), ghost set of votes cast); tuples and frozensets are hashable, so states can go into a visited set.

codeWalkthrough.title: Actions
codeWalkthrough.detail: `actions(state)` yields every enabled step with a label: time out, become leader with a majority, grant a vote (request and reply delivered atomically), and crash + restart (role and votes lost; votedFor lost unless PERSIST_VOTE).

codeWalkthrough.title: Invariants
codeWalkthrough.detail: `election_safety`: no two leaders share a term (Raft Figure 3). The build task adds `vote_once` over the ghost log, which a restart cannot erase.

codeWalkthrough.title: BFS
codeWalkthrough.detail: `bfs()` pops states in breadth-first order, checks invariants, records `parent[next] = (state, label)` the first time a state is seen; the first violation found is therefore at the smallest depth, and the trace is rebuilt from parents.

codeWalkthrough.title: Random walks
codeWalkthrough.detail: `random_walks()` takes 1,000 seeded random paths of up to 30 steps - the cheaper alternative, measured against BFS.

codeWalkthrough.title: History checking (lincheck.py)
codeWalkthrough.detail: `check()` keeps call/return entries in a doubly linked list, lifts a call and its return when the register spec allows it, backtracks on a return it cannot explain, and caches (linearized bitmask, state); on failure it names the earliest op outside the longest partial linearization.

checkYourself.a: It visits states in order of distance from the initial state; the first violating state found has the minimal number of steps.

checkYourself.q: Why put VoteOnce on a ghost log instead of on votedFor?
checkYourself.a: A restart erases votedFor, so an invariant over it cannot see the double vote; the ghost log keeps the evidence.

checkYourself.q: What does the memoisation cache key contain, and why is that enough?

title: An order pipeline that survives chaos and proves it
description: One order pipeline built from the earlier labs - bounded admission, idempotency keys, orchestrated saga with recovery, outbox, at-least-once bus, idempotent consumers, W3C tracing and Raft-replicated config - attacked by a bounded chaos campaign and judged by deterministic checks; a local model only explains.
outcome: You can integrate the topic's mechanisms into one system, state its correctness as code-checked invariants, run a bounded chaos campaign, produce a JSON-lines scorecard, and keep a model's explanation honest by checking its claims.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Imports labs/L300/12, 14, 15, 16 and labs/L400/20, 21 by path. Optional: Ollama + qwen2.5:1.5b for a real explanation; Jaeger and the Temporal CLI (manual).
overview: Put every mechanism together, break it on purpose, and let code - not opinion - decide whether customers were harmed.

designBrief.context: A shop takes orders from clients that retry, through a gateway that must not drown, into a saga across orders, payments and shipping that must never keep money for an unshipped order. Other services learn about changes through events. The gateway's limits change at runtime. Faults: courier outages, orchestrator crashes, relay crashes, duplicate deliveries, lost acknowledgements, a flash-sale burst and a config-leader crash.
constraints: 0 audit violations (money kept == amount if shipped, else 0) in every run
Every order reaches a final state; one order and one charge per idempotency key
Every event delivered; every effect (email, revenue booking) exactly once
One trace per order, no orphan spans, valid traceparent headers
Queue never above the committed bound; p99 queue wait <= 6 ticks
Config changes committed through Raft with 0 safety violations; versions never go backwards
Order-level chaos faults touch <= 10% of orders
designBrief.question: How do the mechanisms compose, and how do we prove the composition under faults?

architecture.summary: Clients send orders with an idempotency key and a W3C trace root to a gateway whose queue is bounded by a Raft-committed config value; when full it sheds with 503 + Retry-After. Workers run the L300 orchestrated saga (create, charge, ship; reverse compensation; recover() after a crash). Every step and compensation writes its state change and its event in one outbox transaction, only if the state changed. A relay publishes at least once to a bus that may duplicate; email and revenue consumers keep processed ids with their effects. checks.py reads the services' own data, the outboxes, consumers, spans, queue samples and the Raft log; run_capstone.py turns 27 chaos runs into a 10-criterion scorecard; agent_assist.py lets a local model explain the campaign while code checks each claim.

codeWalkthrough.title: Reuse, not copies
codeWalkthrough.detail: `reuse.py` imports the hardened L300 saga, Raft, backpressure and tracing modules (and lab 20/21 helpers) by path, each with its own helpers.py.

codeWalkthrough.title: Outboxed steps
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Pipeline.outboxed` wraps every saga action and compensation: open a span, run the change and append its event in one `transact`, only if the service's state changed; faults are injected here for cohort orders.

codeWalkthrough.title: Admission
codeWalkthrough.detail: `submit`: a repeated key is an idempotent replay; otherwise the L300 #16 `admit()` queues or sheds with Retry-After, and the client retries later with jitter.

codeWalkthrough.title: Config
codeWalkthrough.detail: `tick_config`: the operator re-proposes `<version>:<max_queue>` every 5 ticks until committed; the pipeline applies committed entries with a newer version only; the leader-crash fault kills the Raft leader at tick 25.

codeWalkthrough.title: Run loop
codeWalkthrough.detail: Each tick: config, arrivals, due retries, up to 3 saga runs (a Crash triggers recover()), relay tick (optionally crashing between publish and mark); the run ends only when everything is final, delivered and the wanted config is committed.

codeWalkthrough.title: Consumers and traces
codeWalkthrough.detail: `email` and `book` run behind IdempotentConsumer; `consumer_span` parses the event's traceparent with the L300 #15 parser and parents its span on the emitting step.

checkYourself.q: Why must an outbox event be written only when the state changed?
checkYourself.a: Recovery re-runs idempotent steps; publishing again would make consumers apply a second, different event id (a second refund booking).

checkYourself.q: The gateway's bound is 1 until the first config commit. Why not use the newest proposed value?
checkYourself.a: A proposed value may never commit (leader crash); only committed, versioned config is safe to act on.

checkYourself.q: The agent says relay-crash 'held=no'. What happens?
checkYourself.a: Code marks the claim WRONG and the scorecard does not change; the model never decides.
